rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet said God neither sleeps nor should sleep, raises and lowers the scales, receives night deeds before day deeds and day deeds before night deeds, and is veiled by fire that would burn all it sees if unveiled.
rows.anchor: قام بيننا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بأربع فقال: «إن الله عز وجل لا ينام،

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: After the prophetic report, Abu Ubayda recited the verse about blessing in the fire and those around it.
rows.anchor: ثم قرأ أبو عبيدة أن بورك من في النار ومن حولها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One explanation takes the blessed one in the fire to mean God's authority and power, and those around it.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه: بورك من في النار سلطانه وقدرته وفيمن حولها.

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others say the blessing concerns Moses and the angels; being in the fire means seeking or approaching it, as ordinary Arabic can name a destination before one reaches its center.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون: هذا التبريك عائد

words: بُورِكَ مَن فِى ٱلنَّارِ وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse blesses Moses and the angels around the fire; God thereby greets and honors Moses, as angels greeted Abraham's household.
rows.anchor: وهذا تحية من الله سبحانه لموسى وتكرمة له كما حيا إبراهيم على ألسنة الملائكة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some identify the fire itself as the recipient of the blessing.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: هذه البركة راجعة إلى النار نفسها.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Mujahid transmitted Ibn Abbas's explanation that the fire was blessed; Ibn Abbas also reported hearing Ubayy recite “Blessed be the fire and whoever is around it.”
rows.anchor: روى ابن أبي نجيح عن مجاهد عن ابن عباس أنه قال: معناه بوركت النار،

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says he heard Ubayy recite “بوركت النار ومن حولها,” supporting the interpretation that the fire itself is blessed.
rows.anchor: سمعت أبيا يقرؤها: أن بوركت النار ومن حولها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the fire-centered interpretation, min can mean ma, and ma can be an extra particle; the resulting sense is blessing upon the fire and those around it, Moses and the angels.
rows.anchor: قد تكون صلة في كثير من المواضع كقوله جند ما هنالك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire is called blessed by analogy with the Qur'an's description of the blessed spot.
rows.anchor: فسمى النار مباركة كما سمى البقعة مباركة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic uses four constructions for blessing: barakaka Allah, baraka fīk, baraka ʿalayk, and baraka lak; an anonymous poem illustrates the forms.
rows.anchor: فإن العرب تقول: باركك الله، وبارك فيك، وبارك عليك وبارك لك، أربع لغات

rows.speaker: أهل الحق
rows.claim: The people of truth hold that God is beyond limits, place, direction, and time, since these are marks of created things; creation belongs to Him and He is exalted above spatial and temporal bounds.
rows.anchor: أن الله سبحانه وتعالى مستغن عن الحد والمكان والجهة والزمان لأن ذلك كله من أمارات الحدث

rows.speaker: أهل الحق
rows.claim: God's attributes cannot move or occupy a place; His speech does not settle in a location and is neither substance, accident, letters, nor sound, but an attribute that excludes muteness and incapacity to speak.
rows.anchor: لم يجز أن يوصف كلامه بأنه يحل موضعا أو ينزل مكانا، كما لا يوصف بأنه جوهر ولا عرض ولا حروف ولا صوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human understanding and hearing may occur in particular places, but they do not encompass the reality of God's attributes; the verse affirms that nothing resembles Him and that He hears and sees.
rows.anchor: فأما الأفهام والأسماع فيجوز أن يكون في موضع دون موضع ومن مكان دون مكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hāʾ in innahu is a supporting pronoun, not a pronoun referring to an entity; the statement continues, “I am God, the Mighty, the Wise.”
rows.anchor: يا موسى إنه الهاء عماد وليست بكناية أنا الله العزيز الحكيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tahtazzu means that the staff moved; jān here is a quick, small-bodied snake.
rows.anchor: فلما رآها تهتز تتحرك كأنها جان وهي الحية الخفيفة الصغيرة الجسم

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the snake was neither small nor large.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: لا صغيرة ولا كبيرة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reconciliation is that the staff first became a jān and later a great thuʿbān, swelling from staff-size into a huge snake.
rows.anchor: أنها في أول أمرها جان وفي آخر الأمر ثعبان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reconciliation is that the snake was swift and light like a jān, while having a thuʿbān's shape and strength.
rows.anchor: أنها في سرعة الجان وخفته وفي صورة الثعبان وقوته

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains that Moses did not look back.
rows.anchor: ولم يرجع، قال قتادة: ولم يلتفت.

rows.speaker: قراءة العامة
rows.claim: The common reading has ḥusnan with ḍamma on ḥāʾ and a sukun on sīn.
rows.anchor: ثم بدل حسنا قراءة العامة بضم الحاء وجزم السين

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads ḥasanan with fatḥa on both ḥāʾ and sīn, after the word “evil.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش بفتح الحاء والسين بعد سوء

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads the exception as God telling Moses that He had frightened him because Moses had killed a man.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن وابن جريج: قال الله سبحانه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says prophets sinned and were punished, then sinned again and God punished them again.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: وكانت الأنبياء تذنب فتعاقب، ثم تذنب والله فتعاقب.

words: إِلَّا مَنْ ظَلَمَ ثُمَّ بَدَّلَ حُسْنًا
rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says God does not frighten prophets over a sin unless one commits it; then God frightens him until he repents. The exception is genuine, and the omitted sense is that whoever repents and replaces evil with good is forgiven.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جريج: فمعنى الآية: لا يخيف الله سبحانه الأنبياء بذنب يصيبه أحدهم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ raises the problem that the sinner who replaces evil with good is forgiven, so why would he remain afraid, and offers two readings.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: يقول القائل: كيف صير خائفا من ظلم ثم بدل حسنا بعد سوء وهو مغفور له؟

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ's first answer distinguishes protected, forgiven prophets who are safe at resurrection from other people, who mix good and evil and thus fear while hoping.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أن تقول أن الرسل معصومة، مغفور لها، آمنة يوم القيامة،

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ's second answer takes the exception as referring to people omitted from the wording: messengers do not fear, but others do; a former polytheist who repents and does good is forgiven and unafraid.
rows.anchor: أن يجعل الاستثناء من الذين تركوا في الكلمة لأن المعنى لا يخاف لدي المرسلون إنما الخوف على غيرهم

rows.speaker: بعض النحويين
rows.claim: Some grammarians say illa means “and” here, citing the exception-like wording about those who wronged in the verse concerning the qibla.
rows.anchor: وقد قال بعض النحويين: إلا هاهنا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some reject taking the phrase as an exception from messengers, whom they consider incapable of wrongdoing; instead, a wrongdoer fears until repentance removes his fear.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: قوله إلا ليس باستثناء من المرسلين لأنه لا يجوز عليهم الظلم

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators say Moses wore a woolen outer garment without sleeves, which explains why he was told to put his hand into its opening.
rows.anchor: لأنه كان عليه في ذلك الوقت مدرعة من صوف، ولم يكن لها كم، قاله المفسرون.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hand emerged white without leprosy or any other affliction.
rows.anchor: تخرج بيضاء من غير سوء برص وآفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hand was one sign among the nine signs with which Moses was sent to Pharaoh and his people.
rows.anchor: يقول هذه آية مع تسع آيات أنت مرسل بهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase omits “sent” before “to Pharaoh and his people,” since the context supplies that word.
rows.anchor: فترك ذكر مرسل لدلالة الكلام عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the midwife left, guards came to search for Moses; his sister warned their mother, who wrapped him and hid him in a hot oven, then lost awareness of what she was doing.
rows.anchor: فقالت أخته: يا أماه هذا الحرس بالباب، فلفت موسى في خرقة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guards saw the oven burning and the mother showing no change of color or milk; she said the midwife was a friend who had visited, and they left.
rows.anchor: ورأوا أم موسى لم يتغير لها لون، ولم يظهر لها لبن،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once her senses returned, the mother learned the baby was still in the oven; God made the fire cool and safe for him, and she lifted him out.
rows.anchor: فقالت لأخت موسى: فأين الصبي؟ قالت: لا أدري، فسمعت بكاء الصبي من التنور،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fearing Pharaoh's persistent search for newborns, Moses's mother felt inspired to buy a small chest from an Egyptian carpenter and cast it into the Nile; she told him she wanted to hide her son and feared Pharaoh's plot, unwilling to lie.
rows.anchor: فقذف الله سبحانه في نفسها أن تتخذ له تابوتا، ثم تقذف بالتابوت في اليم وهو النيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The carpenter twice tried to report her to Pharaoh's slaughterers; God first stopped his speech, then stopped both speech and sight, and the officials beat and expelled him each time.
rows.anchor: وأخذ الله سبحانه لسانه وبصره، فلم ينطق الكلام، ولم يبصر شيئا، فضربوه وأخرجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After falling into a valley, the carpenter vowed not to disclose the child and to guard him; God restored his sight and speech, guided him to Moses, and he believed.
rows.anchor: فجعل لله عليه إن رد لسانه وبصره أن لا يدل عليه، وأن يكون معه لحفظه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's only, beloved daughter had severe leprosy; doctors and magicians said a child found from the sea would heal her if his saliva were applied at a specified sunrise.
rows.anchor: فقالوا له: أيها الملك لا تبرأ إلا من قبل البحر يوجد منه شبه الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the appointed Monday, Pharaoh and Asiya sat by the Nile as the princess played at its bank; servants retrieved the chest, but could neither open nor break it.
rows.anchor: فلما كان يوم الاثنين غدا فرعون إلى مجلس كان له على شفير النيل ومعه آسية بنت مزاحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asiya alone saw a light inside the chest and opened it; Moses lay in a cradle with light between his eyes, and God provided milk through his thumb.
rows.anchor: فإذا هي بصبي صغير في مهده،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God placed love for Moses in Asiya's heart; Pharaoh also loved him, and the princess's application of his saliva cured her leprosy, so she embraced him.
rows.anchor: فألقى الله سبحانه لموسى (عليه السلام) المحبة في قلب آسية، وأحبه فرعون وعطف عليه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's advisers suspected Moses was the Israelite child feared by the regime and had been cast into the river to escape him; Pharaoh moved to kill the baby.
rows.anchor: فقال الغواة من قوم فرعون: أيها الملك إنا نظن إن ذلك المولود الذي نحذر منه من بني إسرائيل هو هذا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asiya pleaded that Moses might benefit them or be adopted as a son; she was childless and asked Pharaoh for him, so Pharaoh gave him to her while saying he himself had no need of the child.
rows.anchor: قالت آسية: قرت عين لي ولك، لا تقتله عسى أن ينفعنا أو نتخذه ولدا، وكانت لا تلد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When news came that Pharaoh had found Moses in the Nile, his mother said he had fallen into the hands of the enemy she had fled; the crisis made her forget God's promise, leaving her heart empty of revelation.
rows.anchor: فأنساها عظيم البلاء ما كان من عهد الله سبحانه إليها

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi explains farigh as forgetful.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي: فارغا أي ناسيا، أبو عبيدة:

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda says her heart was free of grief because she knew Moses had not drowned; the idiom dam fargh describes bloodshed with no retaliation or blood-price due.
rows.anchor: أبو عبيدة: فارغا من الحزن لعلمها بأنه لم يغرق، وهو من قول العرب: دم فرغ إذا كان هدرا لا قود فيه ولا دية.

rows.speaker: العلاء بن زيد
rows.claim: Al-ʿAlaʾ ibn Zayd gives farigh the sense of being alarmed or fleeing.
rows.anchor: العلاء بن زيد فارغا: نافرا، وقرأ ابن محيصن

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن وفضالة بن عبيد
rows.claim: Ibn Muhaysin and Fadala ibn ʿUbayd read faziʿan, with zāy and ʿayn and no alif, instead of farighan.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن وفضالة بن عبيد: فزعا بالزاي والعين من غير ألف،

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take the pronoun in “to disclose it” as referring to Moses: her longing nearly made her reveal that he was her son.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم: الهاء في قوله: به راجعة إلى موسى ومعنى الكلام: إن كادت لتبدي به أنه ابنها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, through ʿIkrima, says she nearly cried out, “O my son!”
rows.anchor: عن عكرمة، عن ابن عباس إن كادت لتبدي به قال: كادت تقول: وا ابناه،

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says she watched the chest rise and fall on the waves, feared Moses would drown, and nearly cried out from compassion.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: لما رأت التابوت يرفعه موج ويضعه آخر، فخشيت عليه الغرق، فكادت تصيح من شفقها عليه،

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says she nearly revealed she was Moses's mother when people later called him Pharaoh's son; distressed, she almost corrected them.
rows.anchor: الكلبي: كادت تظهر أنه ابنها، وذلك حين سمعت الناس وهم يقولون لموسى بعد ما شب: موسى بن فرعون، فشق عليها فكادت تقول: لا، بل هو ابني،

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the pronoun to mean the revelation: Moses's mother nearly disclosed God's revelation that He would return her son.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: الهاء عائدة الى الوحي أي إن كادت لتبدي بالوحي الذي أوحينا إليها أن نرده عليها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God strengthened and steadied her heart, preserving her faith and certainty in His promise.
rows.anchor: قوينا قلبها فعصمناها وثبتناها لتكون من المؤمنين المصدقين الموقنين بوعد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses's sister was named Maryam; quṣṣīhi means follow his trace to learn what happened, as qisas follows one report after another.
rows.anchor: اسمها مريم قصيه ابتغي أثره حتى تعلمي خبره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains seeing him from the side as looking toward something distant while it is beside the observer, without noticing it.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: الجنب أن يسمو بصر الإنسان إلى الشيء البعيد وهو إلى جنبه لا يشعر به.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says she watched Moses as if she did not want him, so that observers would not recognize her interest.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: جعلت تنظر إليها كأنها لا تريده،

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada read ʿan junubin with fatḥa on jīm and a still nūn.
rows.anchor: وكان يقرأ عن جنب بفتح الجيم وسكون النون

rows.speaker: النعمان بن سالم
rows.claim: Nuʿman ibn Salim read ʿan janib, meaning from a side or direction.
rows.anchor: وقرأ النعمان بن سالم عن جانب أي عن ناحية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-maradiʿ is the plural of wet nurses; before his mother arrived, Moses refused every nurse's breast, which alarmed Pharaoh's household.
rows.anchor: وحرمنا عليه المراضع وهي جمع المراضع، من قبل أي من قبل مجيء أم موسى،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses's sister offered to find a household that would take him, nurse and shelter him; the woman had lost her child and longed to care for a baby.
rows.anchor: فقالت لهم: هل أدلكم على أهل بيت يكفلونه لكم أي يضمنونه ويرضعونه ويضمونه إليهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naṣḥ means sincere work free from corruption, the opposite of fraud.
rows.anchor: والنصح: إخلاص العمل من شائب الفساد، وهو نقيض الغش،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Moses smelled his mother, he took her breast; God returned him to her so she would be comforted, cease grieving, and know His promise was true, though most people do not know He promised this.
rows.anchor: فلما وجد الصبي ريح أمه قبل ثديها فذلك قوله: فرددناه إلى أمه كي تقر عينها ولا تحزن

rows.speaker: السدي وابن جريج
rows.claim: Al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj say the guards seized Moses's sister, suspecting she knew him, and demanded his family; she denied knowing him and said only that the household would be loyal to the king.
rows.anchor: قال السدي وابن جريج: لما قالت أخت موسى: هل أدلكم على أهل بيت يكفلونه لكم وهم له ناصحون

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi defines reaching full strength as ages eighteen through thirty.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: الأشد: ما بين ثماني عشرة سنة إلى ثلاثين سنة

rows.speaker: سائر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most commentators put full strength at thirty-three years and say istawā, “became established,” means forty years.
rows.anchor: وقال سائر المفسرين: الأشد ثلاث وثلاثون سنة، واستوى أي بلغ أربعين سنة.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, through Saʿid ibn Jubayr, gives thirty-three for full strength and forty for istiwāʾ, says Adam's descendants were allotted sixty years, and cites the verse about being given time to reflect.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير، عن ابن عباس في قول الله سبحانه: بلغ أشده واستوى قال: الأشد: ثلاث وثلاثون سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wisdom given to Moses means reason, understanding, and knowledge.
rows.anchor: آتيناه حكما عقلا وفهما، وعلما

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid reports the interpretation that the wisdom bestowed on Moses was prophethood.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: قيل: النبوة، وكذلك نجزي المحسنين.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative says Moses called the Egyptian a manifest wrongdoer because he exploited and oppressed people; the author prefers the preceding interpretation as more fitting to the passage's order.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنما قال للفرعوني: إنك لغوي مبين بتسخيرك وظلمك، والقول الأول أصوب وأليق بنظم الآية.

words: أَتُرِيدُ أَن تَقْتُلَنِى كَمَا قَتَلْتَ نَفْسًۢا بِٱلْأَمْسِ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Moses reached to strike the Egyptian; the Israelite saw his anger, feared he meant to kill him, and accused him, though Moses meant the Egyptian.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: ثم مد موسى يده وهو يريد أن يبطش بالفرعوني، فنظر الإسرائيلي إلى موسى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses becoming a tyrant in the land as killing unjustly.
rows.anchor: إن تريد إلا أن تكون جبارا في الأرض بالقتل ظلما

rows.speaker: عكرمة والشعبي
rows.claim: ʿIkrima and al-Shaʿbi say a person is not a tyrant until he has unjustly killed two people.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة والشعبي: لا يكون الإنسان جبارا حتى يقتل نفسين بغير حق.

words: وَمَا تُرِيدُ أَن تَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلْمُصْلِحِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the accusation, the two men separated; the Egyptian understood from the Israelite's words that Moses had killed the earlier Egyptian, informed Pharaoh, and Pharaoh ordered Moses's death.
rows.anchor: فلما سمع القبطي ما قال الإسرائيلي علم أن موسى قتل ذلك الفرعوني، فانطلق إلى فرعون،

words: وَجَآءَ رَجُلٌۭ مِّنْ أَقْصَا ٱلْمَدِينَةِ يَسْعَىٰ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says that when Pharaoh sent executioners, a supporter of Moses took a shortcut from the city's far end, reached him before them, and warned him.
rows.anchor: فلما أرسل فرعون الذباحين لقتل موسى أخذوا الطريق الأعظم فجاء رجل من شيعة موسى من أقصى المدينة

rows.speaker: أكثر أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Most exegetes identify the man as Hizqil ibn Sabura, a believer from Pharaoh's family and Pharaoh's cousin.
rows.anchor: فقال أكثر أهل التأويل: هو حزقيل بن صبورا مؤمن آل فرعون، وكان ابن عم فرعون،

rows.speaker: شعيب الجبائي
rows.claim: Shuʿayb al-Jubbaʾi says the man was named Shamuʿun.
rows.anchor: فقال شعيب الجبائي: اسمه شمعون

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another report gives the man's name as Shamʿan.
rows.anchor: فقال شعيب الجبائي: اسمه شمعون، وقيل:

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says yasʿā means he hurried in his gait to warn Moses.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: يسرع في مشيه لينذره،

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says yasʿā means he walked on his feet.
rows.anchor: مقاتل: يمشي على رجليه، قال يا موسى إن الملأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaʾtamirūna means they intend Moses's death and consult about him; another explanation is that they command one another, as in the verse about agreeing together kindly.
rows.anchor: أي يهمون بقتلك ويتشاورون فيك، وقيل: يأمر بعضهم بعضا نظيره قوله عز وجل: وأتمروا بينكم بمعروف،

rows.speaker: النمر بن تغلب
rows.claim: Al-Nimr ibn Taghlib's verse is cited as evidence for the usage of yaʾtamirūna.
rows.anchor: نظيره قوله عز وجل: وأتمروا بينكم بمعروف، وقال النمر بن تغلب:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses left Pharaoh's city afraid and watching for pursuit, and prayed for deliverance from the unjust people.
rows.anchor: فخرج موسى منها أي من مدينة فرعون خائفا يترقب ينتظر الطلب قال رب نجني من القوم الظالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tiqāʾ Madian means toward and intending Midian, beyond Pharaoh's authority; one says two houses are tiqāʾ when they face each other, and the word comes from liqāʾ.
rows.anchor: أي نحوها وقصدها ماضيا لها، خارجا عن سلطان فرعون، يقال: داره تلقاء دار فلان إذا كانت محاذيتها، وأصله من اللقاء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madyan is not declined because it is the name of a known town.
rows.anchor: ولم تصرف مدين لأنها اسم بلدة معروفة

rows.speaker: قراءة العامة
rows.claim: The common reading has a wāw before Moses's reply; Meccan readers omit the wāw, as do their codices.
rows.anchor: وقال موسى قراءة العامة بالواو، وقرأ أهل مكة بغير واو،

rows.speaker: أهل الكوفة
rows.claim: The Kufans read yakūnu with yāʾ; the remaining readers use takūnu with tāʾ.
rows.anchor: ومن تكون له [قرأ] بالياء أهل الكوفة والباقون بالتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses means that God knows best who brought guidance from Him, distinguishing the one with truth from the one in falsehood.
rows.anchor: بالمحق من المبطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The outcome of the abode is the praiseworthy final state in the afterlife; the unjust, glossed as unbelievers, do not prosper.
rows.anchor: عاقبة الدار أي العقبى المحمودة في الدار الآخرة إنه لا يفلح الظالمون لا ينجح الكافرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh orders Haman to fire clay and make bricks for him.
rows.anchor: فأوقد لي يا هامان على الطين فاطبخ لي الآجر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some say Pharaoh was the first to make bricks and build with them.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه أول من اتخذ الآجر وبنى به.

rows.speaker: أهل التفسير
rows.claim: Exegetes report that Haman gathered fifty thousand builders plus supporting workers, raised a tower higher than any human construction since creation, and Pharaoh tested it by shooting an arrow skyward; it returned stained with blood.
rows.anchor: جمع هامان العمال والفعلة حتى اجتمع خمسون ألف بناء سوى الأتباع والأجراء

words: إِنَّ قَٰرُونَ كَانَ مِن قَوْمِ مُوسَىٰ
rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most commentators say Qarun was Moses's cousin: Qarun's father and Moses's father shared Fāhith, son of Levi, son of Jacob.
rows.anchor: هذا قول أكثر المفسرين، وقال ابن إسحاق

words: إِنَّ قَٰرُونَ كَانَ مِن قَوْمِ مُوسَىٰ
rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq gives another genealogy: Yashhar fathered both Imran and Qarun; Imran's son Moses was therefore Qarun's brother's son, and Qarun his paternal uncle.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إسحاق: تزوج يصهر ابن فاهث شميت بنت تباويت

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says Qarun was called al-Munawwar for his handsome appearance and was the Israelites' finest reader of Torah, but hypocritical like the Samaritan.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: وكان يسمى المنور لحسن صورته ولم يكن في بني إسرائيل أقرأ للتوراة منه،

rows.speaker: المسيب
rows.claim: Al-Musayyib says Qarun served Pharaoh as governor over the Israelites and oppressed them.
rows.anchor: عن المسيب إن قارون كان من قوم موسى فبغى عليهم قال: كان عاملا لفرعون على بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Pharaoh appointed Qarun over the Israelites while Pharaoh was in Egypt.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: كان فرعون قد ملكه على بني إسرائيل حين كان بمصر

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains Qarun's aggression as stemming from his great wealth and many children.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة: فبغى عليهم بكثرة ماله وولده،

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyan, transmitting from Qatada, says Qarun oppressed people through arrogance and ostentation.
rows.anchor: سفيان عنه: بالكبر والبذخ، عطاء الخراساني وشهر بن حوشب

rows.speaker: عطاء الخراساني وشهر بن حوشب
rows.claim: ʿAta al-Khurasani and Shahr ibn Hawshab say Qarun extended his garments by a handspan beyond others.
rows.anchor: عطاء الخراساني وشهر بن حوشب: زاد عليهم في الثياب شبرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mafātiḥ is the plural of miftah, the tool used to open a door.
rows.anchor: وهي جمع المفتح، وهو الذي يفتح به الباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The keys weighed down their carriers because of their heaviness; nāʾa yanūʾu describes rising under a heavy load, as an anonymous poem illustrates.
rows.anchor: أي لتثقل بهم إذا حملوها لثقلها

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid defines the group carrying the keys as ten to fifteen people.
rows.anchor: فقال مجاهد: ما بين العشرة إلى خمسة عشر، قتادة:

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada gives the group as between ten and forty people.
rows.anchor: قتادة: ما بين العشرة إلى أربعين، أبو صالح:

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abu Salih says the group numbered forty men.
rows.anchor: أبو صالح: أربعون رجلا، عكرمة منهم من يقول:

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima reports two estimates: forty or seventy people.
rows.anchor: عكرمة منهم من يقول: أربعون، ومنهم من يقول: سبعون،

rows.speaker: الضحاك عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak, transmitting from Ibn Abbas, says the group numbered three to ten.
rows.anchor: الضحاك عن ابن عباس: ما بين الثلاثة إلى العشرة،

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another estimate puts the group at sixty.
rows.anchor: ما بين الثلاثة إلى العشرة، وقيل: ستون.

rows.speaker: خيثمة
rows.claim: Khaythama says he found in the Gospel that Qarun's keys loaded sixty marked white mules, each key no larger than a finger and each corresponding to a treasure.
rows.anchor: عن خيثمة، قال: وجدت في الإنجيل أن مفاتيح خزائن قارون توقر ستين بغلا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the keys were made from camel hides.
rows.anchor: مجاهد: كانت المفاتيح من جلود الإبل

rows.speaker: يقال
rows.claim: One account says Qarun carried keys everywhere: first iron, then wood when iron was too heavy, then finger-length cowhide keys; forty mules carried them when he rode.
rows.anchor: ويقال: كان قارون [أينما] ذهب يحمل معه مفاتيح كنوزه،

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Some interpret the keys as guards; Abu Salih adopts this interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: أراد بالمفاتيح الحراس وإليه ذهب أبو صالح

rows.speaker: أبو زرين
rows.claim: Abu Zarrin argues that one key would suffice for the people of Kufa, so the verse means Qarun's treasures rather than literal keys.
rows.anchor: عن أبي زرين قال: لو كان مفتاح واحد لأهل الكوفة كان كافيا إنما يعني كنوزه،
